content: 1. Advisory Services and Education: Entities such as agricultural and public health advisory services, farmers and their organizations, pest control operators, and public health workers should actively provide guidance on pesticide management. Users must be encouraged to access educational materials and understand their content before handling or applying pesticides. 2. Promotion of Integrated Pest and Vector Management (IPM/IVM): Governments should make concerted efforts to develop and promote the use of IPM/IVM strategies. Lending institutions, donor agencies, and governments should support the creation of national IPM/IVM policies and improve related concepts and practices. These strategies should involve farmers (including women’s groups), extension agents, on-farm researchers, communities, and relevant public health entities. 3. Stakeholder Collaboration: All stakeholders, including farmers, farmer associations, IPM/IVM researchers, extension agents, crop consultants, the food industry, pesticide manufacturers, pest control operators, public health workers, environmentalists, and consumer representatives, should play an active role in developing and promoting IPM/IVM. 4. Research and Development of Safer Alternatives: Governments, with the support of international and regional organizations, donor agencies, and research funds, should encourage research into alternatives to existing pesticides. These alternatives should pose fewer risks to human and animal health and the environment, such as biological control agents, non-chemical pesticides, and low-risk chemical pesticides that degrade into harmless components after use. 5. Improved Pesticide Application Methods: Governments, the pesticide industry, and equipment manufacturers should develop and promote pesticide application methods and equipment that minimize risks to human and animal health and the environment. These methods should also optimize efficiency and cost-effectiveness. Periodic practical training in these activities should be conducted. 6. Resistance Management: Governments, the pesticide industry, and international organizations should collaborate to develop strategies to prevent and manage pest resistance to pesticides. This includes considering the impact of agricultural pesticide use on resistance development among disease vectors and public health pests. 7. Technical Assistance for Developing Countries: Governments with advanced pesticide regulation programs should provide technical assistance, including training, to other countries to help them develop infrastructure and capacity for managing pesticides throughout their lifecycle. 8. Testing and Quality Control: Each country should have access to facilities to verify and control the quality of pesticides offered for sale or export. This includes testing for active ingredients and formulation suitability according to international or national specifications. Where facilities are lacking, access to laboratories in other countries should be considered. 9. Analytical Laboratory Support: International organizations and other interested bodies should assist in establishing or strengthening analytical laboratories in pesticide-importing countries. These laboratories should adhere to sound scientific procedures, possess necessary expertise, and have adequate analytical equipment and supplies. 10. Post-Registration Surveillance: Governments and the pesticide industry should collaborate on post-registration surveillance and monitoring studies to determine the fate of pesticides and their health and environmental effects under operational conditions. 11. Data Collection and Incident Reporting: Reliable data on health effects and environmental contamination from pesticides should be collected and maintained. Governments should submit incident reports on severely hazardous pesticide formulations to designated national authorities. 12. Pesticide Residue Monitoring: A program to monitor pesticide residues in food, feed, drinking water, and the environment should be implemented. This should align with international standards, such as those of the Codex Alimentarius. 13. Packaging and Labeling: All pesticide containers should be clearly labeled in accordance with relevant regulations or guidelines. Packaging and repackaging should only occur on licensed premises that meet safety standards, ensuring staff protection and environmental safety. 14. Disposal of Obsolete Pesticides: 15. Advertising Regulations: Advertisements should encourage users to read labels carefully and avoid inappropriate incentives for pesticide purchases. 16. International Collaboration: International organizations, governments, and public interest groups should collaborate to provide countries with the information needed to meet the objectives of the International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management. 17. Monitoring and Observance of the Code: Governments, in collaboration with international organizations, should monitor the observance of the Code and report progress. The pesticide industry and NGOs are invited to provide reports on their activities related to the Code’s implementation. 18. Dynamic Nature of the Code: The Code should be periodically reviewed and updated to reflect technical, economic, and social progress. It should be considered a dynamic text requiring continuous improvement. 19. International Policy Instruments: Various international agreements and conventions, such as the Codex Alimentarius, the Montreal Protocol, the Basel Convention, and the Stockholm Convention, provide operational and policy frameworks for pesticide management. These instruments address aspects of the pesticide lifecycle, including distribution, use, and environmental protection.
